content: Dr. Frank Pantridge observed that the majority of deaths from coronary events occurred outside the hospital, not in emergency rooms or coronary care units. He concluded that a coronary care unit confined to the hospital would have minimal impact on reducing mortality rates. Driven by this realization, Pantridge envisioned a coronary care unit that operated within the community. His solution was the development of the world’s first mobile coronary care unit (MCCU). This unit was staffed by an ambulance driver, a physician, and a nurse. Despite facing numerous obstacles, including skepticism from his cardiology colleagues and resistance from hospital authorities, Pantridge pursued his vision with determination. He encountered criticism for sending junior hospital personnel, such as doctors and nurses, outside the hospital, which was considered unconventional and even illegal at the time. The MCCU program began service on January 1, 1966, in Belfast. John Geddes, a cardiology resident at the Royal Victoria Hospital, was part of Pantridge’s team. Geddes and four other residents were responsible for accompanying the ambulance on its calls. Geddes attributed the success of the program to two factors: Pantridge’s remarkable and persuasive personality, which motivated others to participate enthusiastically, and the hospital’s flat layout, which allowed for quick and efficient resuscitation efforts. He later realized that the infrastructure of the hospital played a significant role in the program’s success, as hospitals in other regions often had slower systems that hindered emergency response. The initial results of the Belfast program were published in The Lancet on August 5, 1967. Over a 15-month period, the team treated 312 patients, half of whom had myocardial infarctions (MIs). Remarkably, there were no deaths during transportation. Of particular importance were the outcomes of 10 patients who experienced cardiac arrest, all of whom had ventricular fibrillation. Six arrests occurred after the MCCU arrived, and four occurred shortly before its arrival. All 10 patients were successfully resuscitated and admitted to the hospital, with five being discharged alive. This groundbreaking report highlighted the potential of prehospital emergency cardiac care and inspired similar programs worldwide. The Belfast system was designed to address acute myocardial infarction cases, but it also demonstrated the ability to resuscitate patients whose hearts fibrillated after the ambulance arrived or en route. However, the system was less effective for patients who experienced fibrillation before the emergency call was placed. At the time, it was assumed that most cardiac deaths in the community were due to acute myocardial infarction, without recognizing that ventricular fibrillation could occur without warning or myocardial infarction. The success of the Belfast program, combined with the international readership of The Lancet, led to the rapid adoption of similar MCCU programs in other countries. Within two years, programs were established in Australia and Europe. In 1968, the first MCCU program in the United States was launched by Dr. William Grace at St. Vincent’s Hospital in New York City. This program mirrored the Belfast model, utilizing specially equipped ambulances staffed by physicians to provide advanced resuscitation care at the scene of cardiac emergencies. The team included an attending physician, a resident physician, an emergency room nurse, an ECG technician, and other personnel, all of whom were summoned to the ambulance within a strict 4.5-minute timeframe. Dr. Grace’s program treated 161 patients in its initial phase, with the ambulance typically reaching the scene within 14 minutes. Among the first group of patients, three were treated for ventricular fibrillation, and one survived. While innovative, the program was limited in scope and not nationally scalable. It became clear that an evolution in prehospital emergency care was necessary. The transition from physician-staffed mobile intensive care units to paramedic-staffed units in the United States occurred independently and almost simultaneously in several communities, including Miami, Seattle, Portland, Los Angeles, and Columbus. These programs represented a significant advancement over the Belfast and New York City models. They not only replaced physicians with paramedics but also addressed the broader challenge of sudden cardiac death in the community.
